Been researching the "Backpack is the Tether of onchain stocks" thesis. Some stuff that came up during diligence...

-Tether makes money on its float; Backpack makes a sliver on volume. At the 0.9 bps cost figure, SPCX's entire first month of volume paid ~$97K in trading cost, total, to everyone. This is a key difference (which is noted). The "64% market share" is issuer-level DEX volume on Solana and excludes competitors several times larger.
-The "no incentives" claim is contradicted by Backpack's existing campaigns and the community share still to be distributed when certain milestones are hit. They notably excluded detected wash-trading activities from their prior points campaigns.
-The stock token is a claim on an SPV with jurisdiction-gated redemption (no US, UK, Japan, UAE or Backpack EU) and dividends paid in more tokens, structurally the same as the xStocks setup the thesis mocks. The regulatory tailwinds actually favor issuers and DTCC tokenizing shares directly, which commoditizes wrappers like Backpack. The unified cross-margining could be an advantage, but likely won't last for long. The pitch "redeemable 1:1, transferable to any brokerage" is mostly for a customer who can't use it. The excluded jurisdictions (US, UK, Japan, UAE, Backpack EU) remove the wealthiest retail; a secondary-market buyer who never onboarded has no right at all. The holders who can redeem mostly wouldn't because anyone who wants a real share in a real brokerage can buy it cheaper and cross-margin it on IBKR already.
-The "US-regulated brokerage" footer says services "in your region" run through Trek Brokerage Services Limited, licensed by the Anjouan Offshore Finance Authority in Comoros. Perhaps this is the only option, don't know, worth noting.
-Staking for at least one year gives users a pathway to redeem their tokens for actual company equity (up to 20% of the company's equity pool) as Backpack builds toward a U.S. IPO. Worth knowing, no other comments.
-Many of the other claims I've seen are straw men that don't make any sort of argument that actually matters. "11x cheaper than Robinhood" is vs Robinhood Chain DEX pools nobody uses, at sub-$1K sizes, during US hours. Robinhood fees have changed a lot recently as they've raised the gas limit. The frictionless piece gives no revenue figure or valuation, etc. It has a volume figure in every section ($1.08B first month, $193M week, 64% share, $108M day one, 10,000 holders) and it never mentions the BP token, the latest raise, or the crypto perps and lending book that are the company's actual revenue. The closest it gets is conceptual: the layer "earns from flow rather than float" and "compounds." These absences struck me as odd.

Would love some push back/clarifications here.

(hold no position long or short in Backpack, nor in anyone I'd consider a competitor)

"Potential FCC rules on optical transceivers more likely to come at 3.2T" - $LITE, $AAOI, $COHR, $SIVE.

Morgan Stanley met with Washington officials:

- Restrictions would likely start at 3.2T modules made in China (800g/1.6T would be left alone)

- Potential restrictions would likely keep laser market tight (combining US DSPs + lasers could meet the 65% US value threshold per MS)

- Chinese modules could qualify if 65% of bill of materials is US content. Chinese modules using US DSPs and lasers are already near that level

- Analysts expect the positive impact on laser pricing... to be more important than any broad redistribution of transceiver market share.

- Analysts don't expect this to bottleneck hyperscaler AI buildouts, they name InP substrate supply as the key variable to watch (hello $AXTI ) 

TLDR:

Component suppliers in general are really positive. Like $SMTC probably winner here for TIAs/drivers (I don't think this was listed), maybe $MXL for DSPs too. 

$AAOI another large beneficiary. 

$SIVE is high-key alpha for laser beneficaries since they have "tremendous capacity" coming online, and that points to US foundries (they haven't formally disclosed location). 

Since previous slideshows show 2 US foundries 1 Taiwan foundry (Win Semi) in terms of their capacity partnerships. And it's process of elimination. 

From CIOE Channel checks it does look like they're starting to work with Chinese pluggable players, (so they'd avenues moving forward as US supply chain component beneficiaries). 

Of course $LITE / $COHR would be happy. 

TLDR: Western supply chains for Lasers / DSPs / TIAs / others are already bottlenecked but qualified capacity becomes even more important.
